# About the computational coursework

## Overview of coursework

* There is one piece of computational coursework for MATH5702M Statistical Computing.

* This coursework is worth 20% of the module mark.

* The coursework is available at <https://mpaldridge.github.io/math5702/> or via Minerva,

* The deadline for the coursework ia **Thursday 10 December** at **1400**.
  - (Optional deadline for feedback: Friday 4 December.)

* Feedback on the final report and marks will be returned on Monday 11 January.



## Deadlines

The are two deadlines for this work. 

1. There is the **main submission deadline** which is the penultimate day of term, **Thursday 10 December** at **1400**.
  - Work that is submitted after this deadline will receive a penalty of 5% for every day or part-day late.
  - Work that is more than 14 days late will not be marked and will receive 0.

---

2. *Optionally*, you *may* also wish to get some brief informal feedback on your draft work before the main deadline. *If* you wish to get feedback on your draft work, you should submit that draft by Friday 4 December at 1400.
  - I will return feedback by Monday 9 December.
  - Feedback will be one or two sentences.
  - I will not give a mark to your draft
  - No effect on your mark.
  - No extensions.

## Academic integrity

You must comply with the University's rules on academic integrity <https://students.leeds.ac.uk/academic-integrity> -- most importantly, you work must reflect your own efforts and your own understanding.

See later for comments on use of AI.

## Mitigating circumstances

If you encounter extraordinary unforeseeable personal circumstances that make it impossible for you to submit your coursework on time, you can apply for an deadline extension through the usual mitigating circumstances procedure <https://students.leeds.ac.uk/assessments/doc/mitigating-circumstances>.

## About your report

* Your task is to write a short report in response to the tasks on the coursework sheet.

* Your report should include all the important R code you use and any important plots you draw.
  - Only include the code and figures relevant to your final and best solution.

* All computational work must be done in R.

* You report must end with a declaration of AI use. (See later.)

---

I call your output a "report" because your work should be explained in detail, in full English-language sentences, with your solutions discussed and justified.

The code and figures you include should be an integral part of your report, not just copy-pasted in at random, and should be fully explained within the text.

Other parts of a more formal "report", such as an introduction, literature review, conclusion, references, etc, are not required here.

## Page limit

There is **no page limit** for the report.

I expect that good reports will typically be around 5--8 pages.

* If your report is 4 pages or less, make sure you have completed all the tasks and fully explained your work.
* If your report has 10 pages or more, make sure you are not wandering from the point or including too many unnecessary figures.

## Report format

Your report should be prepared electronically using the one of the following methods and submitted as follow:

* **LaTeX**: submit both the PDF document and also the `.tex` source. (It is not necessary to submit extra files such as pictures.)

* **R Markdown**, **Quarto** and similar: submit both the PDF or HTML document and also the Markdown (`.Rmd` or `.qmd`) source.

* **Microsoft Word**: Word document (`.docx`).


## Where to get help

Places where you can get help with the coursework include:

* In this computer practical session.

* In my office hours: Thursdays 1200--1300 in my office, MRD 9.10n in the "Maths Research Deck".
  - It is unlikely I will have time to discuss computational work at the beginning or end of a lecture, although if your question is *extremely* short you can try.

* By submitting your draft work for optional feedback, as discussed above.


## AI use

My preference is that you do not use AI for this coursework.

The goal of this coursework is for you to learn how to solve longer problems using the computational ideas you have learned in the module. You will learn this most effectively if you do not use AI

. . .

However, the University rules are that AI may be used -- but only in an "assistive role", and only provided you disclose (that is, tell me about) this use.

---

The following uses of generative AI go beyond merely "assistive" and are **totally forbidden**.

* Asking an LLM chatbot how to answer the questions on the problem sheet.

* Getting an LLM to write R code for you.

* Getting an LLM to write the text of your report for you.

---

The following uses of generative AI are only "assistive", and are permitted *provided you tell me that you used generative AI this way* -- although, like I said, I do not recommend it.

* General revision of topics from the module, not particularly tailored to the coursework problems.

* Help with debugging almost-complete R code that you wrote yourself.

* Spell-checking and grammar-checking a report that you wrote yourself.

* Help with LaTeX code, if you choose to write your report in LaTeX.

## AI declaration

All reports must end with a **declaration of generative AI use**.

* If you did not use generative AI at all, this can simply say: *"I did not use generative AI for the coursework project."*

* If you did use generative AI, this should say what system you used, what tasks it performed, and how you prompted it. Declarations like these should be detailed -- perhaps more detailed than you are used to in other work; declarations should be at least one paragraph long, and usually at least 50 words.

--- 

Here are two hypothetical declarations:

**Declaration of generative AI use (1).** *"The only place I used AI in this coursework was to spell- and grammar-check my report. I uploaded my Word document to Copilot, and prompted it: 'Please check this report for spelling and grammar mistakes.' It found 5 spelling mistakes, which I corrected."*

---

**Declaration of generative AI use (2).** *"I used AI to help when I had a bug in my R code that I couldn't fix myself. I copy-and-pasted my R script into ChatGPT, along with the text of the error from RStudio, and asked ChatGPT what the error was. It pointed out that, in drawing a graph, I had written `col = blue` without quotation-marks around `"blue"`. This was the only time I used AI for the coursework."*

---

If...

* I think you may have used AI in a assistive role beyond being "assistive",
* I think you may have used AI more than in your declaration,
* your work contains no AI declaration or an insufficiently detailed declaration,

...then I will invite you to a short meeting where we can discuss your AI use before I mark your work.


# Accessing R

## R/RStudio on University computers

1. **Open the AppsAnywhere portal** This should be a link on the desktop. If invited to run any software, accept.

2. **Load the language R** Search on AppsAnywhere for "R for Windows" (or similar) and launch it. This will (silently) load the language R. It will also open an inferior RStudio-like program called "RGui" -- you can close it.

3. **Launch RStudio** Search on AppsAnywhere for "RStudio" (or similar) and launch it.

You can alternatively use the [Posit Cloud](https://posit.cloud) to access R and RStudio onlin
